html:
The Sintashta and Andronovo cultures were Bronze Age peoples of the Eurasian steppe, from the southern Urals east to Siberia and south into Central Asia, between about 2100 and 900 BCE. Scholars agree they spoke Indo-Iranian languages.

The Sintashta culture, about 2200 to 1900 BCE, came first. Its people lived in small fortified settlements near the Urals, mined and smelted copper, and buried their dead with horses. Its graves hold the earliest spoke-wheeled chariots known, from around 2000 BCE. Ancient DNA shows its people came largely from an eastward movement of the Corded Ware population, who were themselves descended in part from the Yamnaya.

The Andronovo culture grew out of this world and spread across a huge area, from the Urals to the upper Yenisei and down to Tajikistan. Its people herded cattle, sheep and the newly domesticated horses.

Why they matter:

  • They carried the chariot and the horse across Asia.
  • Their languages are the likely ancestors of Iranian languages and of the Sanskrit of the Rigveda.
  • Some groups moved south past the Oxus civilisation and on into South Asia in the Indo-Aryan migrations.

After them, the steppe passed to mounted nomads such as the Scythians and Saka.
